brief: Morgan Stanley answers investor questions on its power shortfall thesis: impact on semis, who secures power, and what narrows the gap. It sizes the US data center power shortfall at 57 GW gross through 2028, 32 GW net of time-to-power solutions, 34% of demanded power. Nvidia's own commentary confirms the shortfall is real and that more chips are being built than there are places to put them, but Morgan Stanley stays convicted Nvidia and Broadcom, with a combined ~$800bn 12-month AI revenue outlook and ~90% XPU share, can still hit their forecasts, since management has visibility into chip placement. Broadcom's FY27 AI revenue guidance rose from above $100bn in March to $115bn in September, less upside than expected, pressuring AMD, though warrant dynamics with AMD's largest customers offset this. Risk instead falls on ASICs, losing share to GPUs on lower tokens per watt. Power access concentrates among credit-worthy hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, SpaceX, CoreWeave, Nebius), forecast at 60-95% of global capacity additions through 2028, squeezing smaller or international players. International expansion and faster behind-the-meter generation could narrow the gap, but not enough abroad capacity exists to absorb the full US shortfall, and labor plus political pushback constrain BTM buildout.
